title: Don’t Let Rogue Scripts Gobble Up Your Customers’ Data
summary: AI-armed attackers don’t take the long weekend off. How to protect customer data from rogue scripts on websites and mobile apps this Thanksgiving.
body_markdown:
*AI-armed attackers don't take the long weekend off. The websites and mobile apps customers use to travel and shop need a defense that doesn't either.*


**The short version:** Thanksgiving starts the busiest stretch of the year for travel and online shopping, and every airline app, hotel booking page and holiday storefront loads code from outside vendors. That code runs on the customer's device, where server and network tools can't see it. Attackers using AI know that holiday staffing is thin and the traffic is heavy. Rogue scripts can gobble up payment details and personal information while customers book trips and shop. Teams that put AI on the client side can help protect that data while their people enjoy the holiday.


## Everyone gets a seat at the table, even the scripts nobody invited


Picture a Thanksgiving table with forty chairs and a guest list nobody has checked since spring. That's a typical checkout page. Analytics tags, chat widgets, payment tools, reviews, A/B testing and ad pixels all pull up a chair, and each one can read what the customer types. Mobile apps work the same way: travel and shopping apps carry SDKs from outside vendors that run with the app's full permissions on the customer's phone.


Most of those guests behave. The trouble is that any one of them can change without warning, because its code lives on the vendor's servers rather than the company's. This month,[OPTIMJACK](https://www.feroot.com/blog/thanksgiving-rogue-scripts-customer-data/) showed what happens when one of them turns. A trusted testing script carried a card skimmer onto the sites of 178 organizations, and none of those organizations changed a line of their own code. Days later,[PaperCut](https://www.feroot.com/blog/papercut-newspaper-card-skimmer-supply-chain-attacks/) did the same to about 80 US newspaper checkouts through a single line added to the payment form they all share.


## Why the long weekend is prime time for AI attackers


Attackers have always liked holidays. Change freezes slow down fixes, on-call teams are stretched, and the traffic spike hides unusual activity. What's new this year is AI. The Director of National Intelligence[warned days ago](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/22/jay-clayton-tech-outages-faa-microsoft-thanksgiving.html) that AI is helping attackers strike at a scale nobody has seen, and the tools that help defenders find flaws help attackers find the weakest script on a checkout page just as fast.


Most of the industry's AI defense has gone to the server room: patching, network detection and identity. That leaves the client side, where customers enter payment details and personal information, watched by quarterly reviews and allowlists that trust a vendor's domain no matter what its code does today.


## Three ways to stop rogue scripts from gobbling up customer data


Security and compliance teams don't need to give up their holiday to close the gap. They need defense that keeps watch on its own.


- **See every guest at the table.** Map every script on login, checkout and account pages, including what tag managers load, and every third-party SDK inside the mobile app.
- **Notice when a guest changes.** Use AI that learns how each script normally behaves and raises an alert the moment one starts reading payment fields or sending data somewhere new.
- **Show the troublemaker the door, and keep the receipts.** Block what shouldn't run on payment pages, and keep the evidence PCI DSS 4.0.1 Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 call for.
